meta.title: Research studio R2: finding out what is already known (the studio's own text)
meta.note: The one-line summaries are the course's own words, written from each paper's abstract on 3 November 2026 (first-pass coding); no abstract is quoted. Paper metadata and counts are in r02-literature-openalex.json (OpenAlex snapshot of the same date). The three-pass worked example reads the open preprint of Hilbers, Brayshaw and Gandy (arXiv 2210.08351, October 2022); check the published version for changes.

question: How do capacity-expansion models stand in for a whole year with a few representative periods, and what happens to storage and to extreme periods when they do?

ladder_q.q: Quote the two words as one phrase and drop the model words. More results, or fewer?
ladder_q.why: The four plain words all had to appear; one phrase alone is a looser condition, even though the words must now sit together.

ladder_q.q: Join three synonyms with OR. More, or fewer?
ladder_q.why: OR widens: a work needs any one of the four phrases.

ladder_q.q: AND the model block. More, or fewer?
ladder_q.why: AND narrows: a work now needs one phrase from each block.

ladder_q.q: AND the word storage. More, or fewer?
ladder_q.why: Another AND narrows again, and it can drop relevant papers whose abstracts use other words.

matrix.name: Poncelet et al. (2016)
matrix.summary: Picks representative days with an optimisation and compares it with clustering and simple rules, using new measures of how representative a set is.

why.storage: The abstract does not mention storage.
why.full: It compares selection methods with each other, not with a full-year model run.

matrix.name: Kotzur et al. (2017)
matrix.summary: Compares aggregation methods across several energy-system designs; the system matters more than the method, and typical periods as usually modelled cannot carry seasonal storage.

why.storage: It names the storage problem; it does not link the periods. Mentioning storage is not the same as modelling it.
why.full: It speaks of the real system cost, but the abstract does not say how that cost was found: a second pass would tell.

matrix.name: Pfenninger (2017)
matrix.summary: Compares downsampling, clustering and simple rules in a Great Britain power model with 25 years of wind and solar data; the best method depends on the data and the model.

why.storage: The abstract does not mention storage.
why.extreme: The abstract names no extreme periods.
why.full: It compares results across methods; the abstract does not name a full-resolution benchmark.

matrix.name: Kotzur et al. (2018)
matrix.summary: Links typical periods through a storage level that carries energy from one period to the next, so seasonal storage can be modelled, and compares with optimising the full year.

why.storage: This is its contribution: a storage state that connects the periods in sequence.
why.extreme: The abstract names no extreme periods.
why.full: It compares with models of the full annual series.

matrix.name: Liu, Sioshansi and Conejo (2017)
matrix.summary: Picks representative days with two hierarchical clustering methods that keep correlations in time and between places, tested on the Texas power system against the full data.

why.storage: The abstract does not mention storage.
why.full: Its investment decisions are compared with those from the full, unclustered data.

matrix.name: Tejada-Arango et al. (2018)
matrix.summary: Adds links between representative days so that long-term storage fits an investment model, and benchmarks it against an hourly unit-commitment model.

why.storage: A transition matrix between representative days carries long-term storage.
why.full: An hourly unit-commitment model is the benchmark.

matrix.name: Mallapragada et al. (2018)
matrix.summary: Compares a model with up to 12 representative days against a time-slice model for Texas, then runs both plans through an hourly operations model.

why.storage: The abstract does not mention storage.
why.full: Both plans are tested in an hourly grid-operations model.

matrix.name: Teichgraeber and Brandt (2019)
matrix.summary: Compares five clustering methods on two operating problems, battery and gas-turbine scheduling; a better clustering score does not always give a better result.

why.storage: The battery runs inside each period; nothing links the periods.
why.full: It compares objective values; the abstract does not say against what.

matrix.name: Sun et al. (2019)
matrix.summary: Groups days by the investment decisions each day would lead to, rather than by the input data alone, for large power systems with many locations.

why.storage: The abstract does not mention storage.
why.full: The abstract names no full-year benchmark.

matrix.name: Yeganefar et al. (2020)
matrix.summary: Adds extreme days of high and low net load to the representative days, picked with self-organising maps, and tests them on two power systems.

why.storage: The abstract does not mention storage.
why.extreme: Extreme days of net load are its contribution.
why.full: It reports better operating-cost estimates; the abstract does not say against what.

matrix.name: Teichgraeber, Küpper and Brandt (2021)
matrix.summary: Adds extreme periods one at a time, using the planning model's own results, until the design meets demand in every hour of the full data.

why.storage: The abstract does not say whether storage links the periods; a second pass would check.
why.extreme: Extreme periods, found from the model's results, are its contribution.
why.full: The design is checked on the full input data.

matrix.name: Reichenberg and Hedenus (2022)
matrix.summary: Measures how representative periods distort cost and capacity results against a full chronological year, in a European model with 90% wind and solar.

why.storage: The abstract does not mention storage.
why.full: A full chronological year is the benchmark.

fillers.name: Hilbers, Brayshaw and Gandy (2023)
fillers.summary: Picks periods after a first model run, keeps the extreme periods that drive capacity, and keeps chronology so storage can be modelled.

fillers.name: Moradi-Sepahvand and Tindemans (2023)
fillers.summary: A clustering-based aggregation that keeps extreme values and the order of days, for planning lines with short- and long-term storage on a six-bus test system.

fillers.name: Moradi-Sepahvand and Tindemans (2024)
fillers.summary: Links day blocks in sequence and keeps extreme values with representative days and hours, in a model that plans lines, storage and wind farms together.

review_summary: Sorts the aggregation methods used in 130 publications by their assumptions, and lists open questions.

gap_q.q: No paper in your twelve both links storage and keeps extreme periods. Is that a research gap?
options: Yes: an empty cell is a gap
No: someone must have done it
Not yet: search that cell directly first

feedback.yes: Not yet. Twelve papers are a sample, and coding from abstracts can miss things. Search the cell itself before you claim it.
feedback.no: Too quick the other way: nobody knows until the cell is searched. Run the search, then read what it finds.
feedback.test: Right. An empty cell is a lead, not a gap. Turn it into a search string and log the result.

passes.label: First pass
passes.read: Title, abstract, introduction, section headings, conclusions; glance at the references you already know.
passes.out: The five Cs: category, context, correctness, contributions, clarity.

passes.label: Second pass
passes.read: Figures, tables and the argument; skip the proofs. Mark the references to read next.

passes.label: Third pass
passes.read: Rebuild the work under the same assumptions, and challenge each one.
passes.out: What you would do differently, and what it would change.

headings: 1. Introduction (capacity expansion planning; time series aggregation; inter-period links and storage)
4. Simulation studies (overview; setup; validation; example; discussion)

five_cs.q: What kind of paper is it?
options: A new method, tested in simulations on a test system
A case study of one real country's plan
five_cs.worked: A methods paper: a new aggregation framework, tested in simulations on a six-region test system.

five_cs.q: Which papers does it build on?
five_cs.worked: Two from your matrix: Kotzur et al. (2018) for linked storage, and Teichgraeber, Küpper and Brandt (2021) for extreme periods taken from model results.

five_cs.q: Which assumptions will you check in pass two?
five_cs.worked: A test system based on the IEEE six-bus system; demand and wind only, no solar; operation with perfect foresight.
Periods chosen after a first model run that keep chronology for storage and keep the extreme periods that drive capacity; models, data and code released.
Your judgement: note one thing you would ask the authors.

sheet.v: Can choosing periods after a first model run cut the error of capacity plans built from long weather series, in models with storage?
A six-region test grid: baseload, peaking and wind generation, transmission and storage, built from scratch.
Hourly demand and wind for European countries, 1980–2017, from a published reanalysis-based dataset.
Capacity-expansion optimisation on representative days, then an operations run over the full series.
Three conventional schemes chosen from the input data alone and, on 3-year samples, the plan from the full series.
30 and 120 representative days; 40 resampled series; unserved energy checked over the full series.
Solar; operation without perfect foresight (named by the authors as an extension).

practice.task: Write two concept blocks for your own question; run five logged strings in OpenAlex and one other database (query, date, count).
Screen titles and abstracts down to about 30 candidates; note why you dropped the rest.
Find one review; snowball backward and forward from it; add what the searches missed.
Do a first pass on 12 papers (about 8 minutes each) and code them in a concept matrix with a written coding rule.
Search your empty cell directly; read the closest paper in a second pass; write the gap statement.
